clue.text: Hang out with horrible characters, becoming like Boris, ironically

indicators.note: becoming means turning into something else, so the letters are rearranged into a new form

parts.note: the characters, i.e. the letters, of the word horrible

explanation.surface: Someone who spends time with nasty types ends up resembling Boris Johnson, the clue says with a wink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'becoming' signals an anagram of HANG OUT plus the letters of HORRIBLE. 'Right Honourable' is the formal title of a Privy Counsellor such as a former Prime Minister; 'ironically' because the setter doubts Boris Johnson's honour.
explanation.definitionFit: As an MP and Privy Counsellor, Boris Johnson is formally styled with this title, which the setter finds hardly apt.

clue.text: Still good, old woman's figure outwardly

indicators.note: outwardly says the figure sits on the outside, wrapped round the other pieces

parts.note: a stat is a statistic, a figure
nan is an informal word for a grandmother, an old woman; the 's is a link

explanation.surface: A grandmother keeps a good figure, at least on the outside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' is the adjective (motionless), not the adverb 'yet'; 'outwardly' signals the figure goes around the other pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Still water does not flow, and stagnant describes motionless water or air.

clue.text: Billy — perhaps initially the best ever

definitions.meaning: a billy is a male ..., so a billy is one example of the answer
the initials of Greatest Of All Time, slang for the best ever

explanation.surface: Someone called Billy might be, in modern slang, the best there has ever been.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is an acronym: G.O.A.T. stands for Greatest Of All Time, a sporting accolade.
explanation.definitionFit: A billy goat is the male animal, and GOAT is modern sporting slang built from initials for the greatest performer.

clue.text: One bar's busy and one's rough

parts.note: A means one, as in a single thing

indicators.note: a busy scene is all bustle and activity, so the letters are shaken into a new order

parts.note: one's can mean one has, which is I've when I is the speaker

explanation.surface: One pub is lively, another is a rough place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'busy' rearranges BARS into BRAS. Read 'one's' as 'one has', i.e. I'VE.
explanation.definitionFit: An abrasive surface scrapes and grinds, so it is harsh and coarse to the touch.

clue.text: Soldiers with major are outstanding

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, a corps of British soldiers
main means chief or principal, as major does

explanation.surface: Troops serving under a major are remarkable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outstanding' here means still to be dealt with, as an outstanding debt, not excellent.
explanation.definitionFit: Tasks that remain have not yet been finished, just like bills still unpaid or pending.

clue.text: Winger studied recording before kick-off

indicators.note: a recording captures the voice, so the past tense of a word is taken as it is said aloud

parts.note: read in the past tense means studied, and it is said like red
the kick-off is the start of a football match

explanation.surface: A football winger watched footage before the match began.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Winger' suggests a footballer, but it is a bird. 'recording' turns READ into its spoken form RED.
explanation.definitionFit: Winged creatures can be called wingers in crosswords, and the redstart is a small songbird.

clue.text: Wound up mate originally in a cunning volte-face

indicators.note: the clue word that signals this step
a volte-face is an about-turn, so the words a cunning are read backwards

parts.note: art can mean craft or cunning

indicators.note: originally points to the opening letter of each of the words up and mate

explanation.surface: Someone got wound up by a friend's sly change of heart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wound up' looks like one phrase but 'Wound' alone is the definition. A + ART turned round by 'volte-face' gives TRAA, with U and M put 'in'.
explanation.definitionFit: Trauma is the medical term for a physical injury, so it is another word for a wound.

clue.text: 'Following ladies sleep around' sounds like a witty comment?

parts.note: next means following, as in the next day

indicators.note: around suggests the letters are moved about into a new order

explanation.surface: A seedy line about women sleeping around is passed off as wit.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is playful: a speaker moving on in a slideshow says this, and 'slide' sounds like a sly remark.
explanation.definitionFit: A lecturer's routine request to a projectionist can be delivered as a dry quip to move past an awkward moment.

clue.text: Start down — you moved left with your back to the wall

definitions.text: with your back to the wall

parts.note: an intro is the start of a song or piece

indicators.note: moved left tells us to shift a letter towards the front of the word for down

parts.note: blue means down, feeling low
U is text shorthand for you

explanation.surface: A sad opening: you shift left and end up cornered against a wall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moved left' takes the U of BLUE to the front, giving UBLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Having your back to the wall is an idiom for being in a difficult or desperate situation.

clue.text: Hoylake's third, middle of green — I fancy chance of eagle here

indicators.note: fancy as an adjective means elaborate or ornamented, so the letters are rearranged
third picks the third letter of the word Hoylake
middle of takes the inner letters of green, dropping its first and last

explanation.surface: A golfer at Hoylake stands mid-green and fancies scoring an eagle.
explanation.walkthrough: Hoylake is a golf links near Liverpool; an eagle is two under par. 'fancy' rearranges Y + REE + I.
explanation.definitionFit: An eyrie is the high nest of a bird of prey, so it is where you might well spot one.

clue.text: Old politician's wife out — heat up meal

indicators.note: out says the letter for wife is taken away from the word for the politician

parts.note: a Whig was a member of an old British political party

indicators.note: up here means stirred or disturbed, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: With his wife out, an old statesman heats up a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: WHIG without W gives HIG; 'up' shuffles HEAT into HTEA.
explanation.definitionFit: High tea is an early evening meal in Britain, usually with cooked food, bread and tea.

clue.text: Charlie, turn key to go outside! Mug!

parts.note: a charlie is a British word for a fool, as is an ass

indicators.note: to go outside says the key is placed around the turn

parts.note: Alt is a key on a computer keyboard
a U is a U-turn

explanation.surface: Someone is told to turn the key and get out, and is called a mug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charlie' and 'Mug' both look like insults for a fool; only 'Charlie' is, and 'Mug' is the verb to rob with violence.
explanation.definitionFit: To mug someone is to attack and rob them, so the verb is a synonym for attack.

clue.text: Cycling articles for celebrity magazine

indicators.note: cycling moves letters round from one end of the word to the other

parts.note: the and a are the definite and indefinite articles

explanation.surface: Pieces about bike riding appear in a gossip magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cycling' moves the T of THE A to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Heat is a British weekly title devoted to gossip about famous people and their lives.

clue.text: In fix, getting nothing after foolishly trusting flipping politicians

indicators.note: after places the fixing piece behind the reversed word
flipping means turned over, so the word for foolishly trusting is read backwards

parts.note: naif means naive, foolishly trusting

indicators.note: In places the word for nothing inside the word for fix

parts.note: to nail something is to fix it in place
FA is short for sweet FA, British slang for nothing at all

explanation.surface: Someone in a jam gets nowhere after naively trusting those dreadful politicians.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flipping' reads as a mild British curse but signals reversal; 'In' signals insertion. Sweet FA is British slang for nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Fianna Fáil is a major political party in Ireland, so its members are politicians.

clue.text: One's well-known but talentless

definitions.meaning: someone who is famous; the 's is is

explanation.surface: A celebrity who has no real gifts.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense splits the answer into two words, NOT ABLE.
explanation.definitionFit: A notable is a prominent person, and someone not able lacks any skill.

clue.text: What do we have to pay? They've been charged a hell of a lot!

parts.words: What do we have to pay?
parts.note: the bill is what diners ask for when it is time to pay
ions are atoms that carry an electric charge

explanation.surface: Diners ask for the total and find they have been charged an enormous sum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'charged' suggests a price, but means electrically charged.
explanation.definitionFit: Billions are thousands of millions, an informal way of saying an enormous amount.

clue.text: Badly wanted to pursue prince (was a tosser)

indicators.note: to pursue places the second piece after the first, following it

parts.note: if you itched to do something you badly wanted to

explanation.surface: A prince is mocked for his eager pursuits, being something of a tosser.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tosser' is a rude British insult, but here it is literal: one who throws, as a pitcher does.
explanation.definitionFit: To pitch is to throw, so someone who pitched has tossed something, like a bowler or thrower.

clue.text: Labour minister, who once attacked political correctness, claims most of others exaggerated

indicators.note: claims means takes in, so the abbreviation holds the next piece inside it

parts.note: PC stands for politically correct

indicators.note: most of drops the final letter from the word for others

parts.note: the rest means the others
OTT is over the top, exaggerated

explanation.surface: A Labour politician known for hitting out at political correctness.
explanation.walkthrough: John Prescott, Labour's deputy leader, famously punched a protester who threw an egg at him in 2001. 'most of' cuts REST to RES.
explanation.definitionFit: John Prescott was Deputy Prime Minister under Tony Blair and once hit a heckler.

clue.text: Manual worker right — there's an unpleasant smell inside

indicators.note: inside places the smell within the other two pieces

parts.note: a hand is a worker, as in farmhand
OK means all right, correct
BO is body odour

explanation.surface: A manual labourer is fine, though there is a bad smell indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Manual worker' reads as one phrase; 'Manual' is the noun for a guide book.
explanation.definitionFit: A manual is a reference book of instructions, the same thing as a guide or guidebook.

clue.text: Last month dons still sick — that's rough!

indicators.note: dons means puts on, so the sick piece wears the month around it

parts.note: uncured means not healed, still ill
ult., short for ultimo, means last month in old business letters

explanation.surface: Academics remained ill all last month, and that is hard luck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dons' looks like university teachers but is the verb to put on.
explanation.definitionFit: Rough here means crude and lacking refinement, as an unsophisticated person is.

clue.text: Islander in secret announcement

indicators.note: in says the answer is found within the words secret announcement

explanation.surface: An islander is involved in a confidential announcement.
explanation.definitionFit: Crete is a large Greek island, and a person from there is a native islander of it.

clue.text: Hairy nude carrying a little weight — not that impressed!

indicators.note: carrying means holding within, so the shuffled word holds the other pieces
hairy means wild or scary, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: W is the short form, little in size, of weight

explanation.surface: A hairy naked person, a bit overweight, fails to impress anyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hairy' rearranges NUDE into UNED, which holds A W.
explanation.definitionFit: Unawed means not filled with wonder or reverence, so not particularly struck by something.

clue.text: Fixes wheels — it prevents issue

indicators.note: wheels means turns round, so the word for fixes is read backwards

parts.note: pins means fixes or fastens

explanation.surface: A mechanic sorts out the wheels, which stops a problem arising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'issue' means offspring; the snip is the slang name for a vasectomy.
explanation.definitionFit: A vasectomy, called the snip, stops a man fathering children, his offspring.

clue.text: Are taking money during period running country

indicators.note: taking means the first piece takes on the money after it

parts.note: an are is a metric unit of area, abbreviated a
M stands for money in economics

indicators.note: during places the running piece within the period

parts.note: an era is a period of time
IC is in charge, as in running a business

explanation.surface: People accept payment while running the nation for a spell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Are' is not the verb but a metric unit of 100 square metres, symbol A.
explanation.definitionFit: America is commonly used as a short name for the United States, a country.

clue.text: Oversight describing short politician as bore

indicators.note: describing means drawing round, so the oversight word encircles the politician

parts.note: care means supervision or oversight
Lib is short for a Liberal

explanation.surface: An official report calls a small politician tedious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bore' suggests a dull person but is the noun for a gun barrel's inside width.
explanation.definitionFit: The calibre of a gun is the internal diameter of its barrel, also called the bore.

clue.text: Dance around, getting suggestive look

indicators.note: around means turned about, so the dance is read backwards

parts.note: a reel is a lively Scottish dance

explanation.surface: Someone dances about and earns a lewd glance.
explanation.definitionFit: A leer is a sly lascivious glance, the sort of look that hints at something improper.

clue.text: Hear about right offering little reward

indicators.note: about means around, so the word for meagre surrounds the letter for right

parts.note: lean means meagre, as in lean years

explanation.surface: Someone hears about a payout that is barely worth having.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hear about' looks like one phrase but splits after 'Hear'.
explanation.definitionFit: To hear of something is to find it out, the sense of discovering news.

clue.text: Turn-on (see models privately)

indicators.note: models as a verb means shapes, so the letters are moulded into a new form

explanation.surface: Something arousing: watching models in private.
explanation.walkthrough: 'models' looks like people on a catwalk but is the verb shapes, rearranging TURNON + SEE.
explanation.definitionFit: This French phrase, meaning between ourselves, is used in English for confidential remarks.
